newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gesamtmetall rejects principle of 32-hour week.
newsitem.headline: Gesamtmetall rejects principle of 32-hour week.

text.p: Germany's engineering employers association Gesamtmetall, responding to a proposal by the IG Metall union, said on Wednesday that it was opposed in principle to the idea of a 32-hour workweek.
"A general 32-hour workweek anchored in pay contracts is rejected in the strongest terms, completely independently of the level of pay compensation offered," the employer group said in a statement.
IG Metall, which currently has a 35 hour week, earlier proposed a move to a 32-hour week as a means to create jobs. It said it would not expect total pay to remain unchanged.

IG Metall successfully negotiated the move to a 35-hour week in the early 1990s, agreed under the terms of the deal that total wages should not be cut even though the working week had been considerably reduced.
But IG Metall head Klaus Zwickel said today he would not expect to be able to push through full pay compensation this time around.

In its response, Gesamtmetall said that it was open to the idea of part-time working where this made sense within a company, but added that a cut in the overall working hours would not be competitve in an international environment.
"Nowhere in the world is a cut in working time used as a means in the battle against unemployment," Gesamtmetall said.
"A general cut in working time has been consciously avoided in precisely those countries which have been more successful than Germany in maintaining and creating jobs," it added.
